verse.text: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
verse.summary: David wrote this as a man who knew what it was to be hunted — armies encamped against him, enemies close enough to "eat up my flesh," as the next verse says. Yet he opens with two questions that are really declarations: if the LORD is my light, darkness has nowhere to hide its ambush, and if He is my strength, nothing in front of me is stronger than what is in me. Notice he doesn't deny the threats exist; he simply measures them against the One standing with him, and they shrink. Whatever you're facing today, ask David's questions out loud — whom shall I fear? of whom shall I be afraid? — and let the answer be: no one.

sermon.title: They That Be With Us Are More
sermon.excerpt: The servant opened the door at dawn and saw an army around the city. Elisha saw the same army and never flinched — because he saw something else too. One short prayer, LORD, open his eyes, and the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire.

bibleStudy.title: Make Haste, and Come Down

verses.text: And Jesus entered and passed through Jericho. And, behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, which was the chief among the publicans, and he was rich. And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature. And he ran before, and climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way. And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house. And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully. And when they saw it, they all murmured, saying, That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner. And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord, Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold. And Jesus said unto him, This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is the son of Abraham. For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.

Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them. And he spake this parable unto them, saying, What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it? And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing. And when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost. I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.
This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.

bibleStudy.excerpt: A rich, hated little man climbed a tree just to catch a glimpse of Jesus — and ended up getting called down by name, into dinner, into a story Jesus still tells about who He actually came for.
body: Start with the math nobody in Jericho wanted to do out loud, but everybody had already done in private: Zacchaeus was rich, and Zacchaeus was a thief, and most of the town considered those two facts to be the same fact stated twice. Luke doesn't bury the description — he puts it right up front, "the chief among the publicans, and he was rich," which in first-century Jericho was not a compliment, it was an indictment with a job title attached. Tax collectors in that system got rich by overcharging their own countrymen, with Rome's muscle standing behind every collection. Zacchaeus hadn't just done that — he'd climbed to the top of doing it, chief among the publicans, meaning every other tax collector in the district answered to the one man in town everybody already despised the most. That's the résumé walking toward the crowd the day Jesus came through Jericho.

And here's what that résumé bought him: nothing, when it actually mattered. "He sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature." Money had built Zacchaeus a house, a staff, probably a seat near the front of every other gathering in that city, because money generally does buy you a seat near the front. It could not buy him three extra inches, and it could not buy him a single friend in that crowd willing to let a man they despised squeeze in beside them for a better view. So the chief tax collector of Jericho, a man who could likely have bought most of that crowd outright, did the one thing his money and his title couldn't do for him: he ran — Luke actually bothers to tell us he ran, which from a dignified rich man in long robes was its own kind of scandal — and he climbed a sycamore tree like a boy half his age, just to see a Rabbi walk by. Here's my real question for you today: what's the one thing in your life right now that your money, your title, and your reputation absolutely cannot buy you access to — and are you still too dignified to run and climb for it?

Jesus does not simply glance up and smile at the strange sight of a rich man in a tree. He stops, He looks up, and He says the one thing in this entire Gospel I think Zacchaeus never saw coming: his own name. "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Not "you up there." Not "sir." Zacchaeus — a name Jesus had never once used before that moment, in a town He was only passing through, called out loud enough for the whole murmuring crowd to hear it. And notice the verb isn't a suggestion — "make haste." Jesus doesn't tell him to come down whenever it's convenient. Grace, when it finally finds you, is rarely leisurely about it. It doesn't knock politely and wait for a better hour. It calls your actual name in front of everybody who's already decided who you are, and it tells you to hurry.

And the crowd does exactly what crowds in Luke's Gospel always do when grace reaches past their approval rating: they murmur. "They all murmured, saying, That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." Catch how precise that complaint is — not "a man who does sinful things," but "a sinner," the label, the whole identity reduced to one category. This is nearly the same complaint, almost word for word, that opens a parable a few chapters earlier in the same Gospel: "Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them." Same crowd, same murmur, same math — they can tally up exactly who Jesus should be eating with, and Zacchaeus's name was never going to make that list. So Jesus answers the murmur the same way both times: not with an argument, but with a story about what He actually went looking for.

"What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?" That parable isn't background information sitting beside Zacchaeus's story — it's the operating manual for it. The shepherd doesn't send a memo to the lost sheep asking it to find its own way back to acceptable behavior and then rejoin the flock on its own merit. He goes after it, into whatever ditch or bramble or sycamore tree it climbed into, and when he finds it, Luke says he "layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing." Rejoicing — not relieved, not merely satisfied the math is fixed, rejoicing, the way heaven apparently feels every single time this exact scene repeats itself. Jesus walked into Jericho that day already carrying the shepherd's math in His chest: ninety-nine respectable people found is not better than one chief tax collector found. Both scenes end in a party nobody comfortable was invited to throw.

Watch what repentance actually looks like once it shows up in Zacchaeus, because it is not a feeling, and it is not a speech about how sorry he is. "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Fourfold — the law only required him to repay what he'd stolen plus a fifth; Zacchaeus volunteers four times the amount, which tells you he wasn't negotiating a settlement, he was emptying a conscience. This is the test every quiet, private "I've changed" eventually needs to pass: does it ever reach your ledger? Zacchaeus didn't just feel differently about Jesus by the time he climbed down from that tree — he reached for his own account books before Jesus even asked him to. That's not works-righteousness buying its way into favor; that's what grace looks like the moment it actually lands on a man who was genuinely found.

And Jesus's verdict over him is the whole sermon in one sentence: "This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is the son of Abraham. For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost." Not "reward that which reformed itself first." Seek and save that which was lost — the same shepherd, the same hunt, the same rejoicing shoulders, now landing on one specific little rich man who thought a sycamore tree would be as close as he'd ever get. And if you want to know how far this reaches past Jericho, listen to a man named Saul of Tarsus, decades later, no longer persecuting churches but planting them, writing to a young pastor named Timothy about his own math: "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief." Chief. The exact word Luke used for Zacchaeus — chief among the publicans — Paul uses on himself: chief of sinners. Two men, two entirely different résumés of guilt, the same title, the same Shepherd, the same ending.

So here's my real question for you today, and I need you to actually sit in it instead of skating past it to the next paragraph: what tree are you still up in, hoping for a glimpse of something you've convinced yourself you're too disqualified to actually meet? Maybe it's not a literal tree. Maybe it's a title you've built that everyone secretly resents you for. Maybe it's a reputation so thoroughly ruined in your own town that you genuinely believe the best you can hope for is to watch from a distance and go home unseen. Zacchaeus climbed that tree expecting a glimpse. He was planning to look at Jesus's back as He walked on, the way every other rich sinner in that crowd got to do, undisturbed, anonymous, safe. He was not expecting to be called by name in front of the exact people most delighted to watch him lose everything.

But that's the whole scandal of this Gospel, repeated so many times you should stop being surprised by it: Jesus does not wait for you to climb down on your own schedule, clean yourself up, and walk over respectably. He stops mid-stride under your tree, says your actual name, and tells you to hurry up and come down, because today — not eventually, today — He's coming to your house. The ninety-nine in the wilderness can wait. The crowd can murmur all it wants. Heaven has already decided that one found sinner is worth throwing a party over, and it has never once asked your hometown's permission first. Come down off whatever you're hiding behind. He already called your name. Make haste — He is not planning on waiting at the bottom of that tree all day. In Jesus' name, amen.

lines: Father, I declare today that they that be with me are more than they that be with them!
I am not outnumbered — I am surrounded by fire!
The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?
Lord, open my eyes, that I may see!
I will not count their horses — I will lift my eyes to the mountain!
Every army that compassed my house is smitten, led away, and sent home finished!
The angel of the LORD encampeth round about me, and delivereth me!
Greater is He that is in me than he that is in the world!
My help was here before my prayer, and it is not going anywhere!
Save this. Speak it over your house today. Fear not — they that be with us are more than they that be with them! In Jesus' mighty name, amen!

dreamFire.title: The Grip That Could Not Hold
dreamFire.intro: Tonight's shield prayer is not a guess at your dream — it meets every hand, spirit, or power that pins you down, seals your mouth, or locks your legs so you cannot run, shout, or wake while you sleep. It does not matter what form the grip takes or where it meets you; it breaks the same way, by the Word and the name of Jesus. Pray it aloud before you close your eyes, in Jesus' name.
points: Father, Your Word declares in Psalm 3:5, "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me" — before any power can pin me down, press on my chest, or hold me still in a dream tonight, I decree that the same sustaining hand already surrounds my lying down and my rising up, and no grip can outlast it, in the mighty name of Jesus!

By the authority of Job 36:16, "...he have removed thee out of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness..." — every narrow, pressing grip assigned to trap me in a strait place in my sleep tonight is broken before it closes, for I am already carried into a broad place no hand can shut me into, in the mighty name of Jesus!

Father, as in Mark 7:35, "...his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain" — every string tied on my tongue to silence me the moment I try to call on Jesus in a dream tonight is loosed now, and I will speak plain the instant I need to, in Jesus' mighty name!

I stand on Luke 1:64, "And his mouth was opened immediately, and his tongue loosed, and he spake, and praised God" — however any power tries to seal my mouth or freeze my voice while I sleep tonight, my mouth opens immediately, and the first word out of it is praise, not panic, in the mighty name of Jesus!

Father, Isaiah 35:6 declares, "Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing" — every leg any power makes heavy, every foot that refuses to run, every voice that goes silent under pressure in a dream tonight receives strength to leap and a tongue to sing, in Jesus' mighty name!

By the record of Psalm 40:2, "He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings" — every pit, every miry clay, every sinking ground set beneath my feet in a dream tonight gives way, for my feet are already established on the Rock, in the mighty name of Jesus!

I decree by 2 Samuel 22:37, "Thou hast enlarged my steps under me; so that my feet did not slip" — no hand on my ankles, no weight on my legs, no grip meant to make me slip or fall in my sleep tonight shall succeed, for my steps are already enlarged, in Jesus' mighty name!

Father, by the pattern of Acts 16:26, "And suddenly there was a great earthquake...and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's bands were loosed" — I call for that same sudden shaking over every band, chain, or hand fastened on me in a dream tonight; let it come without warning and loose me before the grip can tighten, in the mighty name of Jesus!

I take hold of Psalm 118:5, "I called upon the LORD in distress: the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place" — the moment I call on the name of Jesus from inside any tight, pressing, or trapped place in a dream tonight, I am answered and set in a large place before the call is finished, in Jesus' mighty name!

By the cry of Psalm 142:7, "Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name: the righteous shall compass me about" — every dream prison, cage, or holding cell built to keep my soul from rising tonight opens now, and I am compassed about by the righteous, not the wicked, in the mighty name of Jesus!

Father, Romans 8:11 declares that "...he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you" — whatever part of my body any power tries to lock, numb, or paralyze while I sleep tonight is quickened now by the same Spirit that raised Christ from the dead, in the mighty name of Jesus!

I rise on Isaiah 40:29 and 31, "He giveth power to the faint...they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint" — every faintness, every weight, every heaviness pressed on me to hold me down in a dream tonight meets fresh strength, and I mount up, I run, I walk, unpinned and unafraid, in Jesus' mighty name!

So I seal tonight with 2 Corinthians 3:17, "...where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty" — every grip that reaches for me tonight finds only liberty where it expected a prisoner, for the Spirit of the Lord is here, and where He is, I am free. I will wake in the morning loosed in every joint, strong in every limb, and bold in every word, in the mighty, all-consuming name of Jesus Christ, amen! 🔥
